extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and critics of moral philosophy (readers of Popular Science Monthly; students and commentators on Spencer's ethics)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing and critiquing a naturalistic/evolutionary theory of ethics (specifically Spencer's Data of Ethics) for its philosophical adequacy, practical/regulative force, and explanatory method. Emphasizes whether the theory traces moral development, preserves moral distinctions, and can guide real human behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/evolutionary account of morality
rubrics_metrics.description: Morality must be treated as an objective process with a history — i.e., the theory should 'trace the development of morality in the past' and follow it 'through the ages, as it gains in definiteness, in complexity, in range.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a staged narrative of moral development from earliest manifestations to higher social forms; identify the stages through which conduct has successively passed. Use evidence beyond introspection (external sources, comparative biology/history) to reconstruct antecedent conditions and causal chains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of objective scientific method
rubrics_metrics.description: The study of moral phenomena should employ an 'objective method of study' looking at conduct from the outside and 'grasping the enchainement of cause and effect through all past time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground claims in external observation and historical/biological evidence rather than relying solely on individual consciousness. Integrate subjective reports only insofar as they furnish 'safe guidance.' Analogies to physiological processes (digestion, respiration) illustrate limits of introspection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the distinction between right and wrong (preserve moral difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfactory account must not 'do away with the essential distinction between right and wrong' but should explain its rationale rather than abolish it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how the distinction emerges (e.g., by weighing momentary gratification vs. permanent interests or individual vs. social interests) and relate it to life-promoting vs. life-destroying tendencies; avoid reducing morality to mere semantic quibbling or denying normative difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Life-preserving explanatory basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral norms should be explained by their relation to preservation and improvement of life: 'all higher action ... tends to life' and right action is that which 'tends to life, and higher life.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate how ethical rules follow from adaptive interests (individual survival, progeny, social life) and how subordinating transient impulses to longer-term interests promotes both individual and social flourishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accommodation of exceptional cases without overturning general laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory must acknowledge that exceptional influences (e.g., 'the birth of some man of transcendent abilities') may affect history, but treat such exceptions as products of antecedent conditions and not fatal to general laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain exceptional agents as arising from background conditions; allow for admissions about special agencies while maintaining that the main 'stream of human development' follows general patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between general laws and particular 'accidents' of life
rubrics_metrics.description: Good moral theory should distinguish between broad developmental laws and the 'accidents of our life' that occupy consciousness, recognizing that consciousness emphasizes accidents more than laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge and explain particular contingencies/individual motives without letting them obscure the explanatory power of general developmental principles; be explicit about scope and limits of generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory power regarding genesis of action
rubrics_metrics.description: The account should explain how actions are produced — what their essential character and true significance are — by appeal to causation across time and to knowledge of human constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use evidence about bodily constitution, instincts, and past conditioning to explain proximate and ultimate causes of action; avoid relying on simple introspective descriptions of motive as exhaustive explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility with individual consciousness (integration of subjective and objective views)
rubrics_metrics.description: While objective accounts are primary, the theory must 'take account of the direct revelations of consciousness' where they provide safe guidance; it must explain the difference between subjective and objective perspectives on action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how subjective feelings of voluntariness and responsibility relate to objective causal histories; explain why consciousness may mislead about ultimate causes and how to reconcile both viewpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulative efficacy (practical guidance for conduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: A moral system must function as a regulative system for society — i.e., be 'adapted to human wants' and able to influence the mass of society's behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the theory can be taught and communicated effectively, whether it can produce habitual guidance across populations, and whether it performs at least as well as rival systems in producing social order and virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological motivational power / binding force
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory should have sufficient motivational force ('binding force') to move people to action; it must be able to compete with the emotional intensity of theological systems that offered extraordinary rewards and punishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the emotional/persuasive resources of the theory (appeal to life, enlightened self-interest, education) and whether these can sustain moral restraint and aspiration in ordinary people, acknowledging it may lack theology's terror-based leverage but can substitute gentler, rational pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconciliation of self-interest and duty
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral account should reconcile self-interest and duty by showing that 'self-interest merging into duty' leads to the highest rewards desirable by self-interest itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate how enlightened self-interest (e.g., subordinating appetite for health, controlling impulses) prepares individuals for social duties; show mechanisms through which personal self-conquest supports altruistic action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to inspire moral enthusiasm and high aspiration
rubrics_metrics.description: The system should be capable of arousing deep moral passion and striving for excellence ('moral enthusiasm' comparable to religious sanctity) in a portion of humanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue whether, and by what pedagogical and cultural means, a naturalistic/evolutionary ethic can generate intense longing after purity and high character similar to that produced by religious creeds; consider rare but important exemplars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical communicability
rubrics_metrics.description: The success of the theory depends on 'proper means be taken to bring the new system home to people's understandings' — i.e., it must be teachable and presentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess clarity, accessibility, and didactic strategies; evaluate whether theorists can present the ideas so they influence public opinion and daily conduct rather than remaining abstract philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal coherence and non-conflict with observable facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Any additions or extensions to the theory must not conflict with its main positions and should align with observable facts about human nature and history ('anything we may require to add ... will not be found in conflict with the writer's main positions').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for internal consistency and compatibility with empirical data; ensure proposed modifications integrate without contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical realism about limits (acknowledge slow progress and arrears of work)
rubrics_metrics.description: A credible system should be realistic about social change: natural morality will not instantly eradicate crime or replace theology and will 'find some heavy arrears of work on hand.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid utopian claims of immediate transformation; include strategies for gradual reform, reform pedagogy, and acceptance of transitional difficulties; compare historically to periods when theological systems coexisted with vice.
